extracted.intended_audience: experimental physicists / physical scientists investigating absorption of radiant heat by gases and vapors
extracted.subtask_description: Experimental method for detecting and comparing absorption of radiant (obscure) heat by gases and vapors using an intermittent beam (rotating disk) to produce audible tones from contained gases; includes apparatus choices, controls, and manipulations that affect sensitivity and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound-production test for radiant-heat absorption
rubrics_metrics.description: Place gases or vapors in diathermanous bulbs and expose them to an intermittent radiant beam; the presence and intensity of audible musical tones indicate absorption of radiant heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The strength of the sound correlates with the amount of absorption: highly absorbent vapors produce loud tones, weakly absorbent gases produce feeble or no tones. Use this as the principal qualitative assay of absorptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermittent beam generation (rotating slitted disk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce an intermittent (pulsed) beam by rotating a disk with radial slits/teeth across the radiant beam; pulses interacting with absorbent gas generate sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct disk from sheet-zinc with radial slits/teeth, mount vertically on a whirling table, and place bulb immediately behind the rotating disk. The disk's rotation velocity determines pitch; ensure stable rotation for reproducible notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of radiant source and optics
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a radiant source and optical components that preserve the effective (obscure) heat-rays: use silvered mirrors rather than glass lenses when possible, and consider source intensity (Siemens lamp, lime-light, candle, red-hot coal, platinum spiral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glass lenses withdraw the most effectual rays; silvered mirrors (including conjugate mirrors) increase effect and distance. Even a candle or red-hot poker can produce audible tones with proper manipulation; stronger sources yield stronger sounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulb/flask geometry and size
rubrics_metrics.description: The size and shape of the bulb/test-tube affects sensitivity: smaller bulbs (down to 3/4 inch diameter) and bulbs with small stems can yield better effects; flasks of 2–3 inches often give good results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with flask sizes; smallest flasks with a stem bore of ~1/8 inch often yielded superior sounds in these experiments. Ordinary test-tubes may also be suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure vapor (not liquid) is the active medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The audible effect arises from the vapor/gas phase above liquids, not from the bulk liquid itself or a fully liquid-filled cell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If beam impinges upon liquid only (cell filled completely), no sound is produced. Even a small bubble of gas in a closed cell suffices to produce audible tones; therefore ensure presence of vapor or gas in the bulb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish vapor effect from haze/condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that visible haze (partial condensation) is not the cause of sound by removing cloudiness and demonstrating continued sound from invisible vapor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat the liquid beyond boiling to remove visible haze; if sound persists (or intensifies) from perfectly invisible vapor, attribute sound to vapor absorption rather than suspended droplets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dryness and moisture control
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace amounts of aqueous vapor markedly increase audible response; thoroughly dried gases/air are much less responsive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dry flasks by heating in a spirit-lamp before filling with dried air; desiccants (sulphuric acid, fused chloride of calcium, phosphoric anhydride) can remove humidity but some residues behave differently over time. Be aware that opening containers or breathing into flasks restores humidity and sounding power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative ordering by sound intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use relative sound loudness as an ordering principle to rank gases/vapors by absorptivity (e.g., sulphuric/formic/acetic ethers very absorbent; chloroform and bisulphide of carbon weak; carbonic acid, nitrous oxide, olefiant gas increasing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequentially displace gases in the bulb to observe changes in sound intensity and establish comparative absorptivity; record consistent ordering across repeats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent thermometric verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Corroborate sound-based absorbency by converting a flask into a thermometer-bulb: gases producing loud sounds should cause prompt and forcible thermometric displacement on radiant exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the thermometric response as an independent check that audible sounds correspond to heat absorption and associated expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin liquid layer quenching test
rubrics_metrics.description: Interposing a thin layer (~1/8 inch) of volatile liquid in the beam can detach the effective rays and quench the sounds, indicating interception of obscure heat-rays by that liquid layer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use water, formic ether, sulphuric ether, or acetic ether layers to demonstrate quenching. Contrast with bisulphide of carbon rendered opaque to light (with dissolved iodine): if opaque layer does not diminish sound, the effective rays are invisible (obscure) heat-rays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of sound with known absorbers/diathermancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Known diathermanous/athermaneous behavior of substances should align with the sound method: highly athermanous vapors produce loud sounds; diathermanous vapors produce weak sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aqueous vapor, nitrous oxide, olefiant gas are strong absorbers (loud); chloroform and bisulphide of carbon are near diathermanous (weak). Use known data as positive/negative controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity and applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The method is extremely delicate and can detect small quantities of absorbent vapors; with suitable optics and mirrors, audible effects can be obtained at distances (e.g., 20 yards) and with low-intensity sources (candle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider applying the method to detect very small concentrations (e.g., detection of fire-damp in mines). Optimize optics and flask selection for maximum sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confounding from flexible envelopes (soap-bubbles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flexible envelopes (soap-bubbles) do not themselves produce sound when filled with gas because pulses expend on the flexible film; however, bubbles can function as sound-lenses, transmitting exterior sonorous waves to other sensors (flame, reed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use soap-bubbles thoughtfully: as lenses they can modulate external sound responses (e.g., altering flame behavior), but they will not serve as direct sound sources for the radiant-beam test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational parameter: disk rotation sets pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: The pitch of the note produced is determined by the velocity of rotation of the disk (same as a siren effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent rotation speed when comparing pitch across samples; pitch itself is not a measure of absorptivity, only the amplitude (loudness) is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of sample-handling artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening or manipulating bottles/flasks can introduce air/moisture that alters sounding power; wetting interior surfaces (e.g., with sulphuric acid) can enfeeble or destroy sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle samples to preserve dryness/chemical state; record storage/treatment (opened vs undisturbed) because earlier openings can vitiate dryness and cause faint sounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heating to intensify vapor activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying heat to a liquid increases vapor density and generally intensifies the sounds produced upon exposure to the intermittent beam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gently warm samples to generate sufficient vapor when ambient vapor pressure is too low; be cautious of condensation changes and verify absence of haze if attributing sound to vapor.
